overview.body:
**Mahāvairocana** (*vairocana*) ​— Universal ‌Illumination, Cosmic ‌Buddha · ​The Great ​Sun, Light ​of the ​Cosmos — ​is the ‌cosmic Buddha ​of the Avataṃsaka ​vision and ‌the central ​deity of ‌East Asian ​esoteric Buddhism: ‌the Great ​Sun (Japanese ​Dainichi) whose ​body is ​the universe itself, ​and whose ‌teaching is ​that every ‌thing in ​existence is ‌his self-expression.[^1]

​The name ‌compounds *mahā*, ​‘great’, with *vairocana*, ‌‘shining forth, ​illuminating everywhere’, ​from the ‌root *vi-√ruc*, ‌‘to shine’ ‌— Monier-Williams ​glosses *vairocana* ​as ‘belonging ‌to or ​coming from the ​sun, illuminating’, ‌and records ​its use ​as a ‌name of ​the sun ‌and of ​the Buddha ​alike.[^2] Where ​the Pāli tradition ​centres the ‌historical sage ‌[[shakyamuni|Śākyamuni]], the ​Avataṃsaka Sūtra ‌and the ​esoteric lineages ​read the ‌awakening itself ‌as cosmic ‌event: the Buddha ‌under the ​tree is ‌revealed as ​Vairocana, and ​the galaxies ​are his ‌sermon.

PuniCodex ​restores the ​name as **Mahāvairocana** ​and serves ‌its temple ​at [mahāvairocana.com](https://xn--mahvairocana-9mb.com); ​the short ​form *Vairocana* ‌is the ​common scholarly ‌abbreviation. The ​restoration keeps ‌the long ā ​of *mahā*; ‌the plain ‌ASCII *mahavairocana* ​is a ​modern convenience ​of the ​early domain-name ‌system, not ‌an attested ​ancient spelling.[^2]

sources.citation: Buswell, Robert E., ed., Encyclopedia of Buddhism (New York: Macmillan Reference, 2004), s.v. ‘Vairocana’ and ‘Huayan’.
Monier-Williams, Monier, A Sanskrit-English Dictionary (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1899), s.v. vairocana, √ruc.

the-name.body:
The name ​is attested in ‌Devanagari as ‌**महावैरोचन** (IAST *mahāvairocana*): ​*mahā*, ‘great’, + ​*vairocana*, ‘shining ​forth, illuminating’, a ​derivative of *vi-√ruc*, ​‘to shine ‌out’. The shorter ​form *Vairocana* is ​standard in ‌the Avataṃsaka tradition ​and in modern ‌scholarship; the ​full honorific *Mahāvairocana* ‌is the liturgical ​name of ​the esoteric schools, ​whence Japanese *Dainichi ​(Nyorai)*, ‘Great ​Sun (Tathāgata)’.[^1] The ‌semantics are solar: ​this is ‌the Buddha as ​sunlight — not ‌a light ​among lights, but ‌the medium in ​which everything ‌else becomes visible.

​The ASCII form ​*mahavairocana* survives ‌only because the ‌early domain-name system ‌could not ​carry diacritics; it ​is a technological ‌compromise, not ​an ancient spelling. ​The Unicode restoration ‌**Mahāvairocana** recovers ​the long ā ​of *mahā* directly ‌in the ​address bar. Because ‌the restoration preserves ​vowel length ​the ASCII form ​loses, the name ​is classified ‌Tier 1.

The ‌letter-by-letter transformation runs:

​- **m** ‌→ **M** — ​Same, capitalized
- ​**a** → ‌**a** — Same
‌- **h** → ‌**h** — ‌Same
- **a** ​→ **ā** — ‌Macron: long ​/aː/
- **v** ​→ **v** — ​Same
- ‌**a** → **a** ​— Same
- ​**i** → ​**i** — Same
‌- **r** → ​**r** — ​Same
- **o** ​→ **o** — ‌Same
- ​**c** → **c** ‌— Same
- ​**a** → ‌**a** — Same
​- **n** → ‌**n** — ‌Same
- **a** ​→ **a** — ​Same

The ​project holds the ​domain **mahāvairocana.com** (xn--mahvairocana-9mb.com) ‌as the ‌canonical home of ​this name.

sources.citation: Monier-Williams, Monier, A Sanskrit-English Dictionary (Clarendon Press, 1899), s.v. vairocana, mahā.
Getty, Alice, The Gods of Northern Buddhism (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1914), on Vairocana and Dainichi.

pronunciation.body:
The ​reconstructed pronunciation ‌of the ‌name is ​**/mə.ɦaː.ˈʋɛː.roː.tɕə.nə/** — ​Sanskrit Reconstruction.[^1]

​Phoneme by ​phoneme:

- ​**Ma-** — ‌Bilabial [m] ​with short ​[ə]
- ‌**-hā-** — ​Voiced breathy ‌[ɦ] with ​long [aː]; ‌the great ​(*mahā*) that ​the macron ​preserves
- ​**-vai-** — ​Labial approximant ‌[ʋ] with ​the diphthong ‌[ɛː]; from ​vi-√ruc, ‘to ‌shine forth’
​- **-ro-** ‌— Trilled ​[r] with ‌long [oː] ​(Sanskrit o ​is always ‌long)
- ‌**-ca-na** — ‌Palatal affricate ​[tɕ] with ​short vowels, ‌closing the ​adjective ‘illuminating ​everywhere’

For ‌the modern ​speaker, the ​closest approximation ‌is: ‘muh-HAA-vy-ROH-chuh-nuh’ ​— the ‌hā held ​long, the ​rest even.

​Kindred and ​historical forms ‌of the ‌name:

- ​**Sanskrit** — ‌महावैरोचन (mahāvairocana), ​‘the Great ​Illuminator’; short ‌form Vairocana
‌- **Chinese** ‌— 毘盧遮那 ‌(Pílúzhēnà); the ​esoteric 大日如來 ‌(Dàrì Rúlái), ​‘Great Sun ​Tathāgata’
- ​**Japanese** — ‌Dainichi Nyorai
​- **Tibetan** ​— rNam ​par snang ‌mdzad (Nampar ​Nangdzé), ‘the ​One Who ​Appears in ‌Every Form’

​Mahāvairocana is ‌Tier 1 ​because the ‌long ā ​of *mahā* ‌is lost ‌in ASCII. ​The name ​is a ​solar formula; ​its length ‌is the ‌stress of ​‘great’.

sources.citation: Monier-Williams, Monier, A Sanskrit-English Dictionary (Clarendon Press, 1899), s.v. vairocana.

domains.body:
**Mahāvairocana** ​is the ‌Buddha ‌whose body ​is ​the ​cosmos: the ​dharmakāya ​made personal, ‌the ​light by ​which ‌every other ​light ‌is ​seen.[^1]

### ‌The ​Cosmic Body

​The ​Avataṃsaka vision: ​the ​universe in ‌all ​its ‌interpenetrating parts ​is ‌Vairocana's body; ​every ‌atom reflects ​every ‌other, and ​the ​net ‌is his ‌sermon.

‌### The ​Great ​Sun

As ‌Dainichi ​he is ​the ‌centre ​of the ​esoteric ‌maṇḍalas — ​womb ‌and vajra ​— ​the ​source from ​which ‌the four ‌directional ​Buddhas radiate.[^2]

‌### ​The Dharmakāya

​In ‌the ‌trikāya doctrine ‌he ‌names the ​truth-body ‌itself: what ​[[shakyamuni|Śākyamuni]] ​the man ​awakened ‌to, ​Vairocana eternally ​is.[^3]

​### Universal ‌Interpenetration

​The Huayan ​teaching ​of the ‌mutual ​containment ‌of all ​things ‌— Indra's ​net ‌— is ‌his ​theology: no ​thing ​exists ​except in ‌relation ‌to all ​things.

sources.citation: Cleary, Thomas, trans., The Flower Ornament Scripture: A Translation of the Avatamsaka Sutra (Boston: Shambhala, 1993).
Hakeda, Yoshito S., trans., Kūkai: Major Works (Columbia University Press, 1972).
Buswell, Robert E., ed., Encyclopedia of Buddhism (Macmillan Reference, 2004), s.v. ‘Trikāya’.

symbols.body:
The ​iconography of ‌Mahāvairocana ‌is ​the iconography ​of ​the centre:[^1]

​- ​**The wisdom-fist ‌(chiken-in)** ​— ​Right fist ‌clasping ​the raised ‌left ​forefinger: the ‌esoteric ​gesture ​of the ​union ​of beings ​with ‌the ​cosmic Buddha, ‌Dainichi's ​signature mudrā
‌- ​**White radiance** ‌— ​His ‌body is ​white ​or golden-white: ‌sunlight, ‌the colour ‌of ​no ​colour, outshining ‌the ​hues of ​the ‌four ​directional Buddhas
​- ‌**The lion ​throne** ‌— Seated ​on ​a ​lotus borne ​by ‌lions at ‌the ​centre ‌of the ​maṇḍala: ​kingship of ‌the ‌dharma-realm
- ‌**The ‌solar ​disk** — ‌The ​Great Sun ​behind ​and within ‌the ​icon: ​the Avataṃsaka's ​light ‌that ‘shines ​throughout ​the ​ten directions’
‌- ​**The two ‌maṇḍalas** ​— The ‌womb-realm ​(taizōkai) ‌and vajra-realm ‌(kongōkai) ​maṇḍalas together ​figure ​his universe: ​compassion's ‌matrix ‌and wisdom's ​diamond

sources.citation: Getty, Alice, The Gods of Northern Buddhism (Clarendon Press, 1914); Hakeda, Yoshito S., trans., Kūkai: Major Works (Columbia University Press, 1972).

mythology.body:
Vairocana's mythology ​is not a ‌life but a ‌revelation: the story ​of what the ​universe looks like ​when seen from ​within awakening.[^1]

### The ​Avataṃsaka Vision

The ‌Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra — ​the ‘Flower Garland’, ​longest and most ‌visionary of the ​great sūtras — ‌is set in ​the second week ‌after [[shakyamuni|Śākyamuni]]'s awakening: ​while the sage ​sits silent under ​the tree, the ​bodhisattvas see the ​truth he is ‌seeing, and it is ​Vairocana. Every particle ‌of the cosmos ​contains every Buddha-field; ‌every being is ​pregnant with awakening; ‌the whole of ​existence is one ‌interpenetrating luminosity, and ​its name is ​Vairocana. The Gaṇḍavyūha, ‌the sūtra's vast ‌closing chapter, sends ‌the pilgrim Sudhana ​through fifty-three teachers ​to learn that the ‌totality he sought ​was never elsewhere.[^2]

​### The Lotus-World ‌(Brahmajāla Sūtra)

The ​Brahmajāla Sūtra gives ​the vision its ‌most quoted image: ​Vairocana seated on ‌a lotus of ​a thousand petals, ​each petal a ​world of a ​hundred million worlds, ‌each with its own ‌Śākyamuni teaching innumerable ​beings — ‘this ‌very world is ​the lotus-world of ​Vairocana’. The historical ‌Buddha is here ‌one flower on ‌the cosmic Buddha's ‌throne.[^3]

### The ​Esoteric Enthronement (Mahāvairocana ‌Sūtra)

The Mahāvairocanābhisaṃbodhi-tantra ​(Taishō 848), translated ​into Chinese by ​Śubhakarasiṃha and Yixing ‌in 724 CE, made ​the cosmic Buddha ​the centre of ​systematic ritual Buddhism: ‌the womb maṇḍala, ​the initiations, the ​seed-syllable a (the ​unborn sound, first ‌letter and first ​principle). Carried to ‌Japan by Kūkai ​in 806, it ‌became the charter ​of Shingon — ‌‘Great Sun’ Buddhism ‌— and the doctrine ​of sokushin-jōbutsu, buddhahood ​in this very ​body, by union ​with Dainichi through ‌the three mysteries ‌of body, speech, ​and mind.[^4]

sources.citation: Buswell, Robert E., ed., Encyclopedia of Buddhism (Macmillan Reference, 2004), s.v. ‘Vairocana’.
Cleary, Thomas, trans., The Flower Ornament Scripture (Shambhala, 1993).
Brahmajāla Sūtra (Brahmā's Net Sūtra), on the lotus-world of Vairocana.
Mahāvairocanābhisaṃbodhi-tantra (T. 848); Hakeda, Yoshito S., trans., Kūkai: Major Works (Columbia University Press, 1972).

syncretism.body:
Vairocana's ​receptions ‌are national ‌in ​scale. ​In China ​the ​Huayan ​school built ‌its ​entire ​philosophy — ‌the ​interpenetration ‌of principle ​and ‌phenomena, ​Indra's net ​— ​on ​his sūtra; ​in ‌Japan ​Kūkai's Shingon ‌made ​Dainichi ‌the sun ​at ‌the ​centre of ‌religion, ​and ​the medieval ‌honji-suijaku ‌synthesis ‌went further, ​identifying ​the ‌Great Sun ​with ​Amaterasu, ‌the sun ​goddess ​of ‌Ise: the ​cosmic ‌Buddha ​and the ​imperial ​ancestress ​read as ‌one ‌light ​under two ‌names.[^1]

​In ​Tibet, rNam ‌par ‌snang ‌mdzad heads ‌the ​five ‌Jinas at ​the ​maṇḍala's ​centre, with ‌[[akshobhya|Akṣobhya]] ​east ​and [[amitabha|Amitābha]] ​west ‌among ​his radiations. ​The ​name ‌also travelled ​as ‌a ​personal one: ‌the ​great ‌eighth-century Tibetan ‌translator ​Vairocana, ​first monk ​of ​Tibet, ‌carried it ‌into ​history.[^2]

sources.citation: Buswell, Robert E., ed., Encyclopedia of Buddhism (Macmillan Reference, 2004), s.v. ‘Huayan’, ‘Shingon’, ‘Honji Suijaku’.
Getty, Alice, The Gods of Northern Buddhism (Clarendon Press, 1914).

cultural-legacy.body:
Two ​of the ‌largest ‌Buddha images ​on ​earth are ​Vairocana, ​and that ​is the ‌measure ​of his ​cultural ‌weight. The ​Fengxian ‌temple colossus ​at ‌the Longmen ​caves ​(completed 675 ​CE, ​patronized by ​the ‌future Empress ​Wu Zetian) ‌and ​the Great ‌Buddha ​of Tōdai-ji ‌at ​Nara (dedicated ‌752, ​the consecration ​attended ‌by monks ‌from ‌across Asia) ​both ​gave the ‌cosmic Buddha ​a ​civic body: ‌the ​empire and ​the ‌early Japanese ​state ‌each proclaimed, ​in ​bronze and ​stone, ​that the ‌universe itself ‌is ​Buddhist.[^1]

The ‌intellectual ​legacy is ​equally ‌monumental: Huayan ‌interpenetration ‌philosophy — ‌every ​thing containing ‌every ​thing — ​remains ​one of ‌the most ​sophisticated ​accounts of ​relatedness ‌in world ​thought, ​and finds ​modern ‌echoes wherever ​systems ‌thinkers reach ​for ‌a native ​Buddhist ‌idiom of ‌interdependence. In ​Japan, ​Dainichi is ​still ​the daily ‌sun ‌of Shingon ​practice.[^2]

sources.citation: Buswell, Robert E., ed., Encyclopedia of Buddhism (Macmillan Reference, 2004), s.v. ‘Longmen’, ‘Tōdaiji’, ‘Huayan’.
Cook, Francis H., Hua-yen Buddhism: The Jewel Net of Indra (University Park: Pennsylvania State University Press, 1977).

archaeology.body:
Vairocana's ​monumental record ‌is ‌the finest ​of any ​Buddha's. ​At **Longmen** ​near ​Luoyang, the ‌Fengxian temple's ​Vairocana ​— seventeen ‌metres ​of Tang ‌limestone, ​flanked by ‌disciples, bodhisattvas, ​and ​guardians — ​survives ​in its ​original ‌open-air niche, ​the high-water ‌mark ​of Chinese ‌Buddhist ​sculpture.[^1] At ‌**Nara**, the ​Tōdai-ji ‌Daibutsu (Birushana ​Butsu) ​was cast ‌in ‌eight pourings ‌of bronze ​and ​consecrated in ‌752 ​in a ​ceremony ‌that drew ​ten thousand ​monks; ‌though twice ​recast, ‌the hall ​and much ​of ​the head ​preserve ‌the Nara-period ‌work, ​and the ‌temple's very ​name ​proclaims the ‌Avataṃsaka ‌vision — ‌Tōdaiji ‌is the ​cathedral of ‌Kegon ​(Huayan) Buddhism.[^2]

​The ​Shingon record ‌adds the ​ritual ​dimension: Tō-ji's ​lecture ‌hall in ​Kyoto ​houses the ​three-dimensional maṇḍala ‌of ​twenty-one esoteric ‌deities ​with Dainichi ‌at ​its centre, ‌installed under ‌Kūkai's ​direction — ​the ​cosmic Buddha ​not merely ‌depicted ‌but architecturally ​enthroned.[^2]

sources.citation: McNair, Amy, Donors of Longmen: Faith, Politics, and Patronage in Medieval Chinese Buddhist Sculpture (Honolulu: University of Hawai'i Press, 2007).
Buswell, Robert E., ed., Encyclopedia of Buddhism (Macmillan Reference, 2004), s.v. ‘Tōdaiji’, ‘Shingon’.

meditation.body:
Vairocana ​is the ‌largest ‌idea ​Buddhism ever ​had: ​that ​nothing is ​outside. ‌The ​historical Buddha's ​insight ‌— that ​things ‌arise ​only in ‌dependence ​— ​becomes, at ​Avataṃsaka ​scale, ​a cosmos ‌with ​no edge ‌and ​no ‌waste, where ​every ‌particle ​is a ‌Buddha ​preaching ​and every ‌being ‌is already ‌lit.

​The ​temptation is ‌to ​treat ​this as ‌metaphysics. ​The ​tradition insists ‌it ​is optics: ‌the ​difference ​between Vairocana's ​world ​and ‌ours is ‌not ​the ‌world but ​the ​eyes. Sudhana ‌walks ‌through ‌fifty-three teachers ‌and ​finds ‌the totality ​was ​never ​elsewhere; the ‌Great ​Sun was ​shining ​the ‌whole time. ​The ​question ​the name ‌asks ​is ‌not ‘do ​you ‌believe in ​the ‌cosmic ‌Buddha?’ but ​‘what, ​in ​this room, ​are ‌you ‌still calling ​ordinary?’

sources.citation: Cleary, Thomas, trans., The Flower Ornament Scripture (Shambhala, 1993).

pali-canon.body:
**The ​cosmic ‌Vairocana is ‌absent ​from ​the Pāli ​Canon.** ​The ​Tipiṭaka knows ‌no ​Buddha ​by this ‌name ​and ‌no ​doctrine of ‌a ​universe-body; ​its centre ​is ​the ​historical [[shakyamuni|Śākyamuni]] ‌and ​the ‌community he ​taught. ‌The ​name ‌*Virocana* does ​occur ‌in ​early Buddhist ​literature, ‌but ‌borne by ‌an ​asura ​chief — ‌a ​different ​figure ‌entirely, a ​caution ​against ‌confusing the ​solar ‌Buddha ​with the ​Pāli ​demigod ​of ‌the same ‌sounds.[^1]

​The ‌canon does, ​however, ​preserve ‌the seeds ‌the ‌Mahāyāna ‌grew: the ​Buddha's ‌refusal ​to ​be defined ​by ‌his ​body, the ​teaching ​that ‌whoever sees ​the ​Dhamma ​sees the ‌Buddha, ​and ‌the ​cosmology of ‌innumerable ​world-systems ‌are all ‌Pāli ​materials ​from which ​the ​Avataṃsaka ‌vision would ‌be ​built.[^2]

sources.citation: Buswell, Robert E., ed., Encyclopedia of Buddhism (Macmillan Reference, 2004), s.v. ‘Vairocana’.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.87 (Vakkali Sutta): ‘whoever sees the Dhamma sees me’.

mahayana-sutras.body:
Three ​canons of ‌texts ‌define him. ​The ​**Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra** ​is ​the ​revelation itself: ‌the ​awakening week ​re-read ‌as cosmic ​disclosure, ‌with the ​Gaṇḍavyūha's ‌pilgrimage of ​Sudhana ​and the ​Daśabhūmika's ​ten stages ​as ‌its ​longest movements ‌— ​the sūtra ‌exists ​in no ‌single ​Sanskrit whole ‌but ​in the ​great ‌Chinese translations ‌of ‌Buddhabhadra (60 ​scrolls, ​c. ‌420) and ​Śikṣānanda ​(80 scrolls, ‌c. ​699).[^1] The ​**Brahmajāla ‌Sūtra** supplies ​the ‌lotus-world image: ​a ​thousand-petalled lotus, ​each ​petal a ‌world, ‌each ​world with ‌its ​Śākyamuni — ​Vairocana's ‌throne as ‌the ‌architecture of ‌everything.[^2]

​The **Mahāvairocanābhisaṃbodhi-tantra** ‌(T. ​848, translated ​724 ​CE by ‌Śubhakarasiṃha ​and ​Yixing) and ​the ‌Vajraśekhara cycle ​translate ​the vision ​into ‌ritual: the ​womb ‌and vajra ​maṇḍalas, ‌the seed-syllable ​a, ‌the three ‌mysteries ​— ​the textual ​foundation ​of all ‌East ‌Asian esoteric ​Buddhism.[^3]

sources.citation: Cleary, Thomas, trans., The Flower Ornament Scripture (Shambhala, 1993).
Brahmajāla Sūtra.
Mahāvairocanābhisaṃbodhi-tantra (T. 848); Giebel, Rolf W., trans., The Vairocanābhisaṃbodhi Sutra (Berkeley: Numata Center, 2005).

commentarial-tradition.body:
The ​commentarial traditions ‌are ‌national ​schools. In ​China, ​the ​**Huayan** patriarchs ​— ‌Dushun, ​Zhiyan, Fazang, ​Chengguan, ‌Zongmi — ​built ‌on ​the Avataṃsaka ‌a ​complete ​philosophy of ​interpenetration: ​the ​fourfold dharma-realm, ‌the ​mutual non-obstruction ‌of ​phenomena, ‌Indra's net, ​taught ‌with ​the famous ‌hall-of-mirrors ​demonstration ​Fazang staged ‌for ‌Empress Wu.[^1]

‌In ​Japan, ​**Kūkai** (774–835) ‌carried ​the ​esoteric canon ‌home ​from ​Tang China ‌and ​wrote its ‌exegesis ​himself: ​the Sokushin-jōbutsu-gi ​(‘Attaining ​Enlightenment ‌in This ‌Very ​Body’) ‌and the ​Unji-gi ​(‘The Meanings ‌of ‌the ‌Sound Hūṃ’) ‌read ​the ‌universe as ​Dainichi's ​own ​discourse — ‌letters, ​sounds, and ​things ​as ‌the Buddha's ​three ​mysteries ​teaching without ‌pause. ​The ‌commentary on ​the ‌Mahāvairocana Sūtra ​by ‌Śubhakarasiṃha ‌and Yixing ​remains ​the ​root exegesis ​for ‌the ‌whole esoteric ​tradition.[^2]

sources.citation: Cook, Francis H., Hua-yen Buddhism: The Jewel Net of Indra (Pennsylvania State University Press, 1977).
Hakeda, Yoshito S., trans., Kūkai: Major Works (Columbia University Press, 1972).

original-script.body:
The ​name is ‌preserved ‌in ​Devanagari as ​**महावैरोचन** ​— ​Brahmic abugida, ​attested ‌Buddhist ​Sanskrit, in ​the ‌Avataṃsaka ​and tantric ‌manuscript ​traditions; ‌the script ​is ​written ​left-to-right.[^1]

The ​scholarly ​transliteration ‌is *Mahāvairocana* ​(IAST), ‌giving ​the normalized ‌reading ​/mə.ɦaː.ˈʋɛː.roː.tɕə.nə/.

‌The rendering ​proceeds ‌step ​by step:

​- ‌Sanskrit ‌Mahāvairocana is ‌written ​महावैरोचन ​in Devanagari: ‌महा ​(mahā) ​+ वैरोचन ‌(vairocana); ​the ​diphthong ai ‌in ​वै is ‌the ​guṇa ​grade of ​the ​root ‌vowel.
- ‌The ​compound ‌is mahā ​(‘great’) ​+ ‌vairocana (‘shining ‌forth’), ‌from ‌vi-√ruc, ‘to ​shine’.
‌- ​IAST encodes ​the ​long ‌ā with ​the ​macron; ​the palatal ‌c ​is ​the affricate ​/tɕ/.
‌- ​The Unicode ‌restoration ​Mahāvairocana ‌is registrable ​in ‌.com; ‌the Devanagari ​form ​is ​not supported ​in ‌the ‌.com IDN ​table.[^2]

sources.citation: Monier-Williams, Monier, A Sanskrit-English Dictionary (Clarendon Press, 1899), s.v. vairocana, √ruc.
Edgerton, Franklin, Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit Dictionary (Yale University Press, 1953), s.v. vairocana.
